basic_info.name: Yolo HealthATM (also branded HealthATM; supplied by Health ATM India Pvt. Ltd. / 'Yolo Health')
basic_info.description: Yolo HealthATM is a made-in-India self-service health kiosk that bundles integrated medical-IoT devices (BP, blood glucose, ECG, haemoglobin, body composition, SpO2, temperature, etc.) behind a touchscreen to measure 25-100+ parameters in a few minutes, then issues an instant screening report and offers teleconsultation. The single most load-bearing fact for MediKiosk is the scope of what it does NOT do: it measures the body, not the story - there is no conversational history elicitation, no digitisation of paper prescriptions or lab reports, and no physician-ready structured clinical summary; its output is a vitals/lab test report plus, in the companion app, an AI-generated plain-language explanation of those test results. At the same time it is the closest Indian prior art on deployment and ABDM posture: the vendor claims 750+ HealthATM installations, ~4.47 million tests, ~248k registered patients and 30+ clients, sells primarily through state-government/smart-city tenders (UP, Arunachal Pradesh, Punjab, Rajasthan, Lucknow, Ayodhya, NHA premises), holds an ABDM-integrated certificate badge and does ABHA creation/record linkage - i.e. it proves the offline-capable patient-facing kiosk form factor and the government procurement channel are real, while leaving the pre-consultation history-and-summary lane entirely open.
basic_info.organization: Health ATM India Pvt. Ltd. (brand 'Yolo Health'); roots in Medical IoT research at IIT Bombay; founders/MD Vinayak Kumar, CEO Pradeep Sonkar; partner non-profit Yolo Health Foundation. Corporate office Mumbai; R&D Bengaluru; production Lucknow and New Delhi.
basic_info.country: India (primary market; also reports deployments in Africa and the Middle East)

technical_features.what_it_does: The kiosk performs autonomous primary/preventive screening: the user identifies themselves (optionally via ABHA), follows an on-screen/touch interface and an operator/attendant, and integrated diagnostic devices measure 25-100+ parameters depending on model - vital signs (BP, pulse, SpO2, temperature), anthropometry and body composition (height, weight, BMI, body fat, visceral fat, muscle/bone mass, metabolic age), blood glucose and haemoglobin, ECG/cardiology, and basic lab/point-of-care tests. It then generates an instant 'health screening report' delivered by print, email, SMS, WhatsApp or the companion app and offers a teleconsultation with a remote doctor (integrated with the government e-Sanjeevani portal in Arunachal Pradesh) for advice/prescription. Newer app features add an AI-generated plain-language health summary of the user's own test results and an AI report chatbot. Critically for Module C, it does not elicit a narrative medical history, does not ingest or digitise external paper documents, and does not produce a physician-ready structured clinical summary or FHIR OPConsultRecord-style document - its 'summary' is an explanation of the device's own vitals/lab measurements.
technical_features.architecture: A kiosk-class edge device: high-resolution camera + touchscreen + a metal/FRP enclosure housing multiple medical-IoT measurement modules, driven by an on-board computer and vendor software, with an optional operator/attendant. Device data flows to a cloud backend that stores reports and patient records, feeds a companion mobile app (YoloHealth Plus, Android at least) and enables teleconsultation and EHR/record linkage. Marketing describes an 'Open API Interoperable framework' aligned to ABDM, an ABHA creation/verification and record-linking layer, and (in the app) AI-generated health summaries and an AI report chatbot. Vendor does not publish the AI models, ASR/OCR stack, database or server architecture, so the internals are a black box.
technical_features.inputs: Human-measured biosignals and point-of-care samples captured by onboard devices (BP, glucose, haemoglobin, ECG, SpO2, temperature, body composition, etc.); user/patient identity details for report delivery and optional ABHA linkage; in the companion app, user-supplied meal photos for nutrition logging. It does not consume clinician dialogue, paper prescriptions, lab report images, or historical FHIR data.
technical_features.outputs: An instant 'health screening report' / test report (parameters, values and 'personalized recommendations') delivered via print, email, SMS, WhatsApp or app; ABHA-linked records where enabled; in-app AI-generated plain-language health summary and AI report chatbot answers; teleconsultation/prescription through the remote-doctor service. No FHIR Composition/Bundle, no coded clinical note and no physician-attested summary document is documented.
technical_features.standards_compliance: ABDM integration is claimed and evidenced at the certificate level: the vendor site displays an 'ABDM Certificate' badge, and the NHA ABDM partner registry lists an entry (appearing as 'ATM India Private Limited', consistent with Health ATM India) under Health Tech with an integration completion date of 10/09/2024. The company describes its direction as 'Open API Interoperable' aligned to ABDM, and the app supports ABHA ID creation and record linking. However, no source confirms the specific ABDM milestone level, no NRCeS/OPConsultRecord FHIR IG conformance is claimed, and there is no evidence of FHIR R4 profile validation, SNOMED CT or LOINC coding of its outputs - the compliance is at the ABHA/identity-and-integration layer, not at a structured clinical-document-summary layer. [Exact ABDM milestone level and FHIR coding conformance: uncertain - not documented]
technical_features.offline_capability: The measurement step itself is local (onboard devices plus kiosk computer), so a screening can be performed without connectivity, but the documented workflow depends on the cloud/network for report delivery (email/SMS/WhatsApp/app), teleconsultation, EHR integration and ABHA record linkage. No published offline store-and-forward, local encrypted store, or later-sync mechanism is described. [Offline sync/store-and-forward behaviour: uncertain - not documented]
technical_features.languages_supported: Primarily English, with Hindi used in vendor communications and Devanagari customer-facing material; kiosks are deployed in Hindi-belt states. No formal published list of UI/voice languages or Hinglish/code-mixed support for the kiosk is available. [Full language support matrix: uncertain]
technical_features.deployment_model: Physical kiosk hardware deployed at the point of care or point of presence - primary/community health centres and PHCs, smart-city public locations (parks, railway/bus stations), municipal corporation sites, corporate offices, hotels/events and the NHA premises - with an operator/attendant in many government deployments. Product variants: wall-mount/desktop (34 params), standard standing model in metal/FRP (60+ params, expandable to 100+), 'Kompact' portable bag (25 params) and a Mobile Medical Unit. Hosted report/records backend is cloud-based via the vendor/app. Exact compute (CPU/RAM) inside the kiosk is not published.

performance_metrics.accuracy_or_quality_metrics: No peer-reviewed or published accuracy, sensitivity/specificity, concordance or error-rate figures for the device measurements or for the AI-generated health summary were located across this sweep. The vendor markets accuracy as a value proposition and cites user satisfaction, not measured performance. [Any accuracy/validation figure: uncertain - none published]
performance_metrics.latency: Operational/product-level timing only: a Korean-market-agnostic railway deployment advertises a 6-minute basic check (16 params) and a 9-minute check (18 params), and vendor material says 60+ parameters are detected 'in just a few minutes'. No latency benchmark for report generation or AI summary is published, and no hardware context (CPU/RAM) is given.
performance_metrics.resource_requirements: Not published. The kiosk is a bundled hardware+devices product; the vendor discloses no CPU class, RAM, storage or model-size requirements for the AI features. This matters because Module C must run on a ~4GB CPU/iGPU kiosk, so Yolo's hardware budget cannot be reused as evidence.
performance_metrics.scale_metrics: Vendor homepage claims 750+ HealthATM installations, 4,469,760+ tests done, 30+ clients and 248,320+ registered patients. Named public-sector volumes include ~266 kiosks for UPMSCL (Uttar Pradesh), 98 advance units in Arunachal Pradesh PHCs (2022), 100 FRP units for Lucknow Smart City (Dec 2021), 18 in Ayodhya (since Jan 2024), plus 20 Punjab and 15 Rajasthan cited in the 2023 launch release, and an official UP government supplier list showing Health ATM India Ltd delivering 240+26 units in the 2023 UPMSCL tender. The same 2023 release also claims 1000+ HealthATMs deployed in Africa and the Middle East. Company size is small (LinkedIn: ~40-50 employees; a separate HealthATM India entity listing shows 1-10).
performance_metrics.evaluation_protocol: None located. There is no published study, controlled comparison, validation against a clinical reference standard, health-economic evaluation, or independent audit of measurement accuracy or of the AI summary. Evidence is limited to vendor case pages, government tender awards and testimonials. For Module C this is the same 'deployed but unmeasured' pattern seen across the category, and it means Yolo cannot be cited as evidence that kiosk-generated content is clinically accurate.

milestone_significance.relevance_to_module_c: Yolo HealthATM is the domestic, offline-capable, ABDM-badged proof-of-concept for the kiosk form factor and the government procurement channel that MediKiosk wants - and simultaneously the clearest demonstration of the complementary gap MediKiosk's Module C is meant to fill. It validates that Indian state governments will buy and run patient-facing health kiosks at scale (750+ installs, UPMSCL/Arunachal/Lucknow/Ayodhya, even the NHA's own premises) and that ABHA/ABDM integration at the identity-and-record-linking layer is achievable and expected. But its capabilities stop at measuring vitals and labs and explaining those numbers; it performs no conversational history elicitation and no paper-document digitisation, and emits no structured, coded, physician-ready consultation summary. That means the entire Module C problem - turning a history bundle plus digitised documents into one NRCeS/OPConsultRecord-conformant bilingual summary with per-field provenance and physician attestation - is unaddressed by the closest deployed Indian comparator. For a Ministry of Ayush/AIIA pitch this is strategically important: the 'measure the body, not the story' framing shows MediKiosk is not a redundant Health ATM clone.
milestone_significance.what_to_adopt_or_reject: Adopt: (1) the operational model of an operator-supervised, kiosk-based screening flow with touch and a companion app - evidence that non-digital users can complete a multi-step kiosk interaction in a public facility; (2) the government-tender and smart-city go-to-market (UPMSCL, Nagar Nigam, NHA premises, Convergence/Smart Cities expos) as the realistic channel; (3) the ABHA-first identity/linkage pattern and the visible ABDM certificate badge as the minimum credibility bar; (4) multi-channel report delivery (print/SMS/WhatsApp/app) as a bilingual output expectation for Indian users. Adapt: their 'AI-generated health summary' into an attestation-gated, provenance-tagged clinical summary rather than a black-box plain-language explanation - Module C should keep the human-readable layer but bind every statement to a source field and a clinician review. Reject: the vitals-only scope as sufficient for OPD intake (MediKiosk must elicit history and digitise documents), the black-box AI with no published evaluation, and any assumption that a device report equals a physician-ready summary.
milestone_significance.limitations_and_risks: No published accuracy or clinical validation of either the device measurements or the AI health summary; unclear whether the kiosk works end-to-end without connectivity (network is required for reports, teleconsult, EHR and ABHA linkage); no public evidence of NRCeS/FHIR/OPConsultRecord or coded (SNOMED/LOINC) clinical output; ABDM compliance appears to be ABHA/identity-level rather than structured-document-level; small vendor (tens of employees, sub-$1M revenue, ~$235K disclosed funding) and claims such as 1000+ overseas kiosks are unaudited; company/entity naming is inconsistent across sources (Yolo Health, Health ATM India Pvt. Ltd., 'ATM India Private Limited' in the ABDM registry). For Module C, the risk to avoid is inheriting Yolo's unmeasured-AI and thin-standards posture.
milestone_significance.differentiator_vs_medikiosk: Yolo HealthATM and MediKiosk share the kiosk form factor and the Indian public-health market, which somewhat weakens the 'first kiosk' novelty claim but sharpens the functional differentiation. Yolo measures biometrics and explains its own test results; MediKiosk elicits a structured conversational history and digitises physical documents before consultation, so the object of work is entirely different (story and documents versus vitals). Yolo emits a screening report, not an NRCeS FHIR R4 OPConsultRecord Bundle, so MediKiosk's conformant, coded, physician-ready summary emission remains unmatched. Yolo publishes no accuracy evidence and no per-field provenance or physician-attestation contract, so MediKiosk's provenance-plus-attestation storyline still differentiates. What Yolo does erode is the claim that offline-capable, ABDM-integrated patient kiosks are novel in India - that is now clearly table stakes, and MediKiosk should position Module C's value above the measurement layer, not alongside it.

business_info.license: Proprietary commercial hardware+software product; no open-source license. Source and models are closed. No public API terms located.
business_info.pricing: Not published as a standard price list; sold B2B/government via tenders and quotations. The one public price point is the Indian Railways deployment (approx. Rs 50 for a 16-parameter basic check and Rs 100 for an 18-parameter basic+HB+sugar check), which is per-test end-user pricing rather than a device/software licence. [Standard unit/AMC pricing: uncertain]
business_info.funding: LinkedIn company data reports about $235K in total funding and revenue under $1M, with ~40-50 employees; no named venture rounds or investors located. [Investors/round detail: uncertain]
business_info.commercial_status: Commercial private company selling to government and institutional buyers, plus state-government and smart-city programme deployments (public procurement). Not free and not an unpaid project.

competition_ecosystem.competitors: The direct comparator set is other Indian health-kiosk/HealthATM vendors - notably the suppliers sharing the same UPMSCL tender (HAL, Maestroes Electronics & Telecommunication System Ltd, PDK InfraTech LLP) - plus government-platform kiosks and screening camps, and consumer health apps (e.g. HeyDoc AI, Tata 1mg, Practo, ABHA PHR apps) competing for the same patient's health-record and follow-up attention. Its functional overlap with MediKiosk Module C is minimal because none of these emit pre-consultation structured histories or NRCeS-conformant summaries.
competition_ecosystem.integrations: ABDM/ABHA (identity creation and record linkage; ABDM-integrated certificate badge), e-Sanjeevani teleconsultation portal (Arunachal Pradesh PHCs), hospital EHR/record linkage (claimed in the UPMSCL project), report delivery over print/SMS/email/WhatsApp and the YoloHealth Plus mobile app, and an 'Open API Interoperable' framework direction. Not an ABDM HIP/HIU/FHIR-summary producer as far as documented.
competition_ecosystem.ecosystem_notes: Three ecosystem signals matter. (1) The ABDM tailwind is now mainstream for kiosks: the NHA's own premises hosts a Yolo HealthATM, which is strong institutional endorsement of the offline-capable kiosk model. (2) Government procurement is the dominant channel - UPMSCL tender lists, Nagar Nigam/smart-city contracts - so MediKiosk should assume a public-tender path and the need for demonstrable standards conformance and reliability, not just a demo. (3) The category's standards depth is shallow: peers certify ABHA/identity integration but do not produce coded, physician-attested clinical summary documents, leaving the NRCeS/OPConsultRecord layer uncontested by deployed Indian kiosks. Also note consolidation/crowding risk: multiple vendors already compete on the same vitals-screening brief, so MediKiosk should not differentiate on measurement breadth.

history.recent_changes_last_6_months: Relative to this sweep's six-month window (verified 2026-09-16): (1) The most substantive product change is the YoloHealth Plus app update dated Mar 7 2026, which added an AI-Generated Health Summary (plain-language explanation of test results), an AI-Powered Health Report Chatbot, and in-app ABHA ID creation - a clear move from raw device reporting toward AI interpretation, though still scoped to the vendor's own test results rather than clinical history or document digests. Note: the NHA-premises installation and the app's AI summary are the freshest concrete signals; no 2026 H1-H2 government tender award for a new state rollout was found. [Any additional unpublicised 2026 deployments: uncertain]

market_positioning.target_users: Primary buyers are governments and institutions - state health departments/NHM, municipal corporations and smart-city companies, PHCs/CHCs, the National Health Authority, railways, and public-sector hospitals - with enterprise/corporate, insurance, hotel/event and retail/wellness buyers second. End users are walk-in patients/beneficiaries seeking quick preventive screening and teleconsultation in semi-urban, rural and public settings.
market_positioning.market_segment: Diagnostics kiosk / HealthATM - self-service preventive and primary health screening kiosks with teleconsultation. It sits adjacent to, but not inside, patient intake, ambient clinical documentation, PHR interoperability tooling or clinical-summary generation.
market_positioning.positioning_statement: Yolo Health pitches itself as 'Reimagining Digital Healthcare', making quality healthcare 'accessible and affordable for all walks of society' and bridging healthcare-access gaps through 'Open API Interoperable framework based technology'. The HealthATM is framed as a one-stop, 24/7, autonomous/attendant-supported kiosk that detects 60+ (up to 100+) parameters 'in just a few minutes', delivers instant reports and teleconsultation, and is built for primary, preventive and predictive care. The company explicitly positions its roadmap as integrating AI for predictive health models and aligning to ABDM, and it markets a visible ABDM certificate and ABHA support as trust signals.
